sections.title: Five membrane modes combine into one motion
teaching: A rectangular membrane can move in different organized patterns while all four edges remain fixed. Each pattern is a mode. In the first pattern, labeled (1, 1), one broad region moves upward and then downward. The pattern (2, 1) divides the surface into two regions along one direction, with neighboring regions on opposite sides of their resting position. The pattern (1, 2) makes that division along the other direction. The pattern (2, 2) divides the membrane in both directions, producing four alternating regions. The pattern (3, 1) has three alternating regions along one direction. The divisions identify the spatial pattern of movement, rather than separate pieces of membrane.

As each mode oscillates, a region above the resting surface returns through that surface and then lies below it. Adjacent regions separated by an internal stationary line reverse in opposite directions. The fixed outside edges stay in place throughout. Higher spatial complexity therefore means more internal divisions, while the membrane remains one connected surface.

The five frequencies displayed are 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz. These are intentionally assigned illustrative frequencies. They are not the natural resonance frequencies calculated for this rectangular membrane. Their regular spacing makes a harmonic example easy to compare, but the example does not establish that a membrane naturally has an evenly spaced harmonic series. All movement is slowed by a factor of 250 so that the changing shapes can be seen. The frequency labels describe the intended physical oscillations, rather than the slow rate visible during playback.

The panel labeled All 5 modes adds the five displacements at every position and time. Where contributions point in the same direction, they reinforce each other. Where they point in opposite directions, they partly cancel. Because the modes change phase at different rates, their sum keeps changing shape even though the five component patterns remain identifiable. Its vertical magnification is reduced to fit the panel, so comparing its apparent height directly with an individual panel would confuse display scale with physical addition.

The spectrum measures the movement at the marked pickup point. Its horizontal axis is frequency in Hz, and its vertical axis is relative amplitude. The peaks at 100, 200, 300, 400, and 500 Hz have equal heights because the component amplitudes were adjusted to give equal measured contributions at that location. Equal local spectral peaks do not mean that every mode has the same displacement everywhere. The setup uses a rectangular aspect ratio of 1.15 and a pickup 0.23 of the distance across one dimension and 0.31 across the other. The speaker notes specify a common local amplitude scale of 0.55 and a combined-panel vertical scale of 0.057 relative to the individual-panel scale of 0.24. These are settings of the illustration, not universal membrane properties.
issues: The speaker notes explicitly identify the five harmonic frequencies as intentionally assigned, not the natural eigenfrequencies of the rectangular membrane.
The combined surface uses a smaller vertical display scale, and the equal spectral heights are engineered for the selected pickup point.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics
teaching: A string with a fixed bottom and a free top has different restrictions at its two ends. The bottom is a displacement node because it cannot move sideways. The top is a displacement antinode because it can move through a large sideways excursion. In the ideal free boundary used here, the string has zero slope at the endpoint. A frictionless sliding endpoint that maintains tension is one way to understand this idealization.

The first mode has no internal displacement node. Its movement grows from the fixed bottom toward the free top. The next three modes have progressively more internal stationary points and regions that move in opposite directions. During an oscillation, each moving region passes through its resting position, reaches the opposite side, and reverses. A frame in which much of the string looks straight is one phase of that movement, rather than evidence that its mode has stopped existing.

The four modes are labeled 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz. The second mode is the third harmonic of the fundamental, the third mode is the fifth harmonic, and the fourth mode is the seventh harmonic. Mode number counts the allowed patterns in sequence, while harmonic number compares a frequency with the fundamental. They differ because the even harmonics do not satisfy this fixed–free boundary condition.

The lower spectrum has frequency in Hz on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. It contains equal-height peaks at 100, 300, 500, and 700 Hz. Equal modal excitation produces those equal contributions when the mixture is measured at the free end, where all four modes have displacement antinodes. The four upper panels show the component modes separately. Playback slows the physical frequencies by 250, giving visible rates of 0.4, 1.2, 2.0, and 2.8 cycles per second.

The 100 Hz fundamental belongs to this separately tuned example. If the length and wave speed were kept unchanged while a fixed–fixed string became fixed–free, its fundamental would become half as high. Two illustrations that both label their fundamentals 100 Hz therefore include a change in length or wave speed. The shared label alone cannot show that changing the boundary leaves the fundamental unchanged.
issues: The speaker notes state that fixed–fixed and fixed–free examples are separately tuned to the displayed fundamental.
The linked ink originals contain small cyan freehand marks without readable text or an additional explicit question.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes
teaching: A quarter-wavelength joins a displacement node to a displacement antinode. That is the simplest spatial pattern that connects the fixed bottom of this string to its free top. The first mode fits one such packet into the string and is labeled 1 × 100 Hz.

The second mode fits three quarter-wavelength packets into the same length. It begins at a node, passes through alternating antinodes and nodes, and still ends at an antinode. It is labeled 3 × 100 Hz. The third mode fits five packets and is labeled 5 × 100 Hz. The fourth fits seven packets and is labeled 7 × 100 Hz. More packets within the same length mean a shorter wavelength and, at the same wave speed, a faster oscillation.

The numbered packet overlays build those counts in order. Packet 1 occurs in all four modes. Packets 2 and 3 occur in modes 2, 3, and 4. Packets 4 and 5 occur in modes 3 and 4. Packets 6 and 7 occur only in mode 4. Thus the completed counts are 1, 3, 5, and 7, rather than 1, 2, 3, and 4. Adding two quarter-wave packets introduces another node–antinode pair while preserving the required type of endpoint.

An even number of quarter-wave packets would connect a node to another node, rather than to the free-end antinode required here. The odd-harmonic pattern follows from the boundary conditions. The moving curves repeatedly reverse direction while keeping their stationary points in the same spatial locations. The numbered packets divide the standing-wave shape; they are not objects traveling from the bottom of the string to the top.

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes
teaching: Air in a vocal tract can be represented as a chain of moving masses linked by springs. The masses represent air inertia, and the springs represent the restoring effect of compression. The chain is fixed at the left and free at the right. It is a simplified air column with a constrained glottal end and an open lip end.

The blue air elements move back and forth along the length of the chain. They do not move sideways as the string did. When neighboring elements approach each other, that region compresses. When they separate, it rarefies. The movement reverses during the cycle, so the animation depicts an acoustic oscillation rather than a continuous stream of particles traveling out of the mouth.

The upper chain is Mode 1, labeled F1-like and identified as the lowest fixed–free air mode. Its displacement is constrained at the left and grows toward the free right end. The lower chain is Mode 2, labeled F2-like and identified as the next fixed–free air mode. It has an additional internal change in the pattern of motion and compression. In this uniform-tube illustration, Mode 2 oscillates three times as fast as Mode 1. This is the ideal fixed–free comparison used in the demonstration; it does not make every finite mass-spring chain have exact integer-related natural frequencies.

The markers identify positions along the same tract, measured from the glottal side toward the lips. The /a/ marker is one third of the way along, the /i/ marker is two thirds along, and /u/ is at the free lip end. Each location participates in both modes. To understand a constriction there, compare how far the air moves and how much neighboring air compresses in each mode. The first two formants refer to resonances of the air column, rather than the vocal-fold repetition rate.
issues: The right edge of the original video crops part of its uniform-tube heading; the visible labels and motion remain interpretable.
The stated threefold relation describes this idealized uniform-tube demonstration, not arbitrary finite discrete chains.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression
teaching: The row labeled Schwa shows the moving air of the uniform-tube reference vowel. The three lower rows isolate Mode1@F1, Mode2@F2, and Mode3@F3. All four rows represent air along a tube that is closed at the left and open at the right. The upper row also changes over time; it is not a motionless baseline.

Follow one blue circle through several phases to see longitudinal displacement. It moves along the tube, passes back through its usual position, reaches the other side of its excursion, and reverses. To see compression, compare the spacing of neighboring circles within a region. Small gaps indicate compressed air, and large gaps indicate rarefied air. A particle moving far and a region changing density are two different features of the same oscillation.

In the lowest mode, motion is constrained at the closed end and strongest near the open end, while compression changes are strong toward the closed end. Higher modes divide the tube into more alternating regions of motion and compression. Some neighboring regions move in opposite directions, so air can bunch up around a location where local displacement is small. As phase reverses, a compressed region can become rarefied.

The labels F1, F2, and F3 identify three resonances of the same air system. The separate rows make it possible to compare what happens at one tract position for each resonance. A constriction can act strongly on the motion of one mode and on the compression of another because their spatial patterns differ. The drawing therefore supports a location-based explanation of formant changes, rather than a rule that every constriction changes all resonances in the same direction.

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode
teaching: For any marked location in an air-mode animation, distinguish the excursion of an air element from the changing distance between neighboring elements. A large excursion means that local air inertia matters strongly to that mode. Large changes in spacing mean that local compression and its restoring stiffness matter strongly. A single frame with crowded circles identifies compression at that moment; following multiple phases reveals how that compression changes.

The same position can play different roles in Mode1@F1, Mode2@F2, and Mode3@F3. Higher modes contain more alternations along the tube, so a location of strong motion in one mode can lie near a region of strong compression in another. Predicting a perturbation requires identifying both the position and the mode. A motion-dominated mass effect tends to lower the corresponding resonance, while a compression-dominated stiffness effect tends to raise it.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed
teaching: Vowels differ in the shape of the air passage above the glottis. The five side-view images compare where the tongue is high or low and where it is toward the front or back of the mouth. High and low describe tongue height, while front, central, and back describe its position along the mouth. These dimensions help locate a narrowing within the tract.

The vowel in dean is high and front. Its image places a constriction about two thirds of the way from the glottis toward the lips. The vowel in dune is high and back, with the highlighted constriction at the lips. Thus two vowels described as high can differ in the location and shape of the constriction.

The central example done is shown between the front and back extremes and is labeled No constriction. It serves as the relatively unconstricted reference in this comparison. Dan is the low front example, and Don is the low back example. Don has a constriction marked about one third of the way from the glottis. The source does not assign a numbered constriction location to Dan.

The fractions describe distance along the tract starting at the glottis. A one-third constriction is farther back along that air path than a two-thirds constriction, while a lip constriction is at its open end. Changing the constriction position changes which parts of each air mode are affected. The tongue-position categories describe articulation; the motion and compression patterns explain why the articulatory change alters the resonances.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness
teaching: Compressing air increases its resistance to further compression. This is the spring-like part of the acoustic system. A constriction in a region that undergoes strong compression changes therefore strengthens a restoring effect that matters to that mode. When that stiffness contribution dominates, the resonance frequency rises because the displaced air is pushed back more strongly.

The same constriction also has a mass-like effect in the lecture’s perturbation account. Bunching air increases its local density, and the narrowed region changes the effective inertia associated with air motion. Where a mode moves air through a large excursion, that loading matters strongly. If the inertia contribution dominates, the air reverses more slowly and the resonance frequency falls.

These effects do not automatically cancel. The locations with the greatest movement alternate along the vibrating air column with locations having the strongest compression changes. A constriction at one location therefore does not give the same importance to both effects. One mode may be motion-dominated there, while another is compression-dominated.

The tract images connect this reasoning to actual differences in vowel articulation. The relevant question is where the narrowing lies within the air-mode pattern. Identify the local movement and compression for the resonance of interest, then decide which change dominates. Saying only that the tract became narrower leaves out the spatial information that determines the qualitative formant shift.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location
teaching: The uniform air-column comparison places the same /a/, /i/, and /u/ locations on both the F1-like and F2-like modes. The glottal side is fixed at the left, and the lip side is free at the right. Air elements oscillate lengthwise around their usual positions. Regions where neighboring elements approach and separate reveal compression and rarefaction, while a large excursion of an element reveals motion.

Compare one location across the two rows rather than assuming that its acoustic role stays the same. Near the lips, both modes allow strong motion. Farther inside the tube, the F2-like mode has additional spatial alternation, so a position can have a different balance of movement and compression from the F1-like mode. The one-third and two-thirds markers identify the regions used for the back and front constriction comparisons.

The label that Mode 2 oscillates three times as fast as Mode 1 describes the uniform reference demonstration. Perturbing its air distribution changes the resonances according to each mode’s local participation. F1 and F2 are tract resonances; these labels do not make them successive harmonics of the vocal-fold source.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model
teaching: The /u/ comparison places the perturbation at the free lip end. The animation enlarges the masses near that end to represent heavier loading there. The left end remains fixed, and the marked air elements still oscillate longitudinally. The one-third /a/ and two-thirds /i/ markers remain reference positions; the active loading is near /u/ at the right.

At the lip end, both the lowest F1-like mode and the next F2-like mode have strong displacement. Loading a region that moves substantially increases the inertia involved in each oscillation. More inertia makes the air harder to accelerate and reverse, so a cycle takes longer when the mass contribution dominates.

The reasoning is therefore the same for both rows. For Mode 1, motion dominates and F1 decreases. For Mode 2, motion also dominates and F2 decreases. The supported prediction is F1 down and F2 down. The larger moving masses visualize why lip-region loading acts strongly on both modes; they do not indicate that the air travels continuously out through the lips.

This is a qualitative model of the /u/ effect. It links constriction location to dominant local motion and then to the direction of each resonance shift. No measured amount of decrease or numerical before-and-after formant values are supplied.
issues: The page gives schematic qualitative predictions rather than reported experimental measurements.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2
teaching: The /i/ model locates the constriction near two thirds of the distance from the glottis toward the lips. The highlighted section occupies that region in both air chains. The position of the perturbation stays the same across the two rows, while the modes have different spatial organizations.

For the lowest mode, the front region participates strongly in air movement. The mass-like loading of the constriction is therefore dominant. Increasing the effective inertia of that moving part makes the oscillation slower, so F1 decreases.

For the second mode, the same front region has strong spring-like participation through local compression and expansion. Neighboring air elements change their spacing as the oscillation reverses. Here the stiffness effect dominates, making the restoring response stronger and the oscillation faster. F2 increases.

The resulting pattern is F1 down and F2 up. One narrowing can cause opposite changes because F1 and F2 do not move and compress the air in the same places. The general roles of inertia and stiffness stay the same; their relative importance changes with the mode. The animation and revealed reasoning establish the direction of the schematic prediction without providing numerical shifts or a completed experimental test.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern
teaching: The /a/ model moves the constriction to about one third of the tract length from the glottis. The highlighted section is farther toward the fixed left end than the front /i/ region. Both rows receive the perturbation at this same back location.
For the first mode, springiness dominates in that region. The air there undergoes substantial compression changes, so increasing the restoring stiffness makes the oscillation faster. F1 rises.

For the second mode, the back region participates more strongly in mass motion. Loading that moving air increases the effective inertia of the oscillation, so it reverses more slowly. F2 falls. The supported prediction is F1 up and F2 down.

This reverses the /i/ pattern because the perturbation has moved to a different part of the modes. The explanation still follows the same cause and effect. Dominant restoring stiffness raises a resonance, and dominant inertia lowers it. Neither vowel height alone nor the statement that a constriction exists determines both arrows. Its position must be related to movement and compression separately for F1 and F2. The source illustrates that qualitative reasoning and supplies no measured numerical change.
issues: The original video title is cropped at its right edge; the native reasoning explicitly gives the one-third location and F1 up, F2 down.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes
teaching: Air can move back and forth along a tube while neighboring portions become closer together and farther apart. The blue circles represent air elements. Their movement is longitudinal, along the tube. They do not travel along the curved outline used to draw a transverse string. The closed left end constrains displacement, while the open right end allows strong motion.

The row labelled Schwa supplies the air-column reference, and the other rows isolate Mode1@F1, Mode2@F2 and Mode3@F3. These labels identify different resonances of the same air system. The first mode has a broad pattern along the tube, while the higher modes fit more alternating regions into that same length.

During one phase, some neighboring elements bunch together and other regions spread apart. As the motion reverses, those spacings change again. A local group can move together through a large distance while its members remain nearly equally spaced. Elsewhere, neighbors move by different amounts, changing their separation substantially. Large motion and large local compression are therefore different features of a mode.

Those differences explain why location matters. Added effective mass influences a mode most where the air participates strongly in its movement. A change in local springiness matters most where spacing changes create strong compression or expansion. The same location can have different roles in the first, second and third modes, so an acoustic prediction requires examining the particular mode there.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing
teaching: Voiced speech begins with a vibrating source. The source spectrum contains harmonics at successive multiples of its fundamental frequency F0. The three spectra share the same horizontal window from 0 to 4000 Hz, so their different spacings can be compared directly.

For F0 = 100 Hz, the marked sequence begins 100, 200 and 300 Hz and continues in 100 Hz steps. This is associated with big, loose vocal folds. For F0 = 250 Hz, the sequence begins 250, 500 and 750 Hz, with wider spacing, and the accompanying description is tighter, lighter vocal folds. For F0 = 350 Hz, the sequence begins 350, 700 and 1050 Hz, with still wider spacing, associated with very tight, light vocal folds.

Lower F0 places more harmonics within the same frequency window. Higher F0 spaces them farther apart and leaves fewer opportunities to sample the shape of a vocal-tract resonance. These are source spectra before vocal-tract filtering, so their evenly spaced stems should be distinguished from the resonance pattern that a vowel shape adds.

The membrane comparison has fixed edges and five illustrated spatial patterns. Their labels are (1,1), (2,1), (1,2), (2,2) and (3,1), assigned 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz in the illustration. The two indices distinguish divisions along the two surface directions. The final surface combines the five motions and marks a pickup point. These assigned harmonic frequencies illustrate combination and source spacing, rather than establishing equally spaced natural frequencies for every membrane.
issues: The membrane inset repeats an illustrative frequency assignment. Lecture 14 page 2 speaker notes explicitly state that the assigned 100–500 Hz frequencies are not the natural eigenfrequencies of that rectangular membrane. That source qualification applies to the reused illustration here.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics
teaching: The vocal tract changes the relative strengths of the harmonics supplied by the voiced source. Its shape acts as a filter. Resonances favor nearby harmonics, making them more prominent, while harmonics far from the favored regions are weaker. The simplified rule describes the nearby harmonics as audible and the distant ones as muted.

A fixed–free comparison represents one end as closed and the other as open. Changing the vowel shape changes the resonance locations within that arrangement. The MRI views compare an unconstricted central shape, a lip constriction for /u/, a front constriction about two-thirds of the way from the glottis for the row labelled /i/ or /I/, and the open/back comparison for /a/.

The schwa /ə/ example marks resonances at 500 and 1500 Hz. The /u/ example marks 300, 1000 and 2000 Hz. The /i/ or /I/ example marks 300 and 2200 Hz. The /a/ example places two closely spaced marks at 800 and 900 Hz. The common horizontal frequency axes extend from 0 to 4k Hz, where 1k means 1000 Hz.

The marked resonance frequencies describe the filter. They do not mean that the source must generate a harmonic exactly at every mark. The actual harmonics remain determined by F0, and their relative strengths depend on how closely they fall to the favored filter regions. The voiced source supplies the harmonic locations, while vowel shape determines which frequency regions are emphasized.
issues: The /a/ labels overlap slightly, but original-resolution inspection resolves two separate marks at 800 and 900 Hz. These schematic targets differ from other supplied vowel illustrations and are retained for this page.
The source row is printed as /i/ or /I/. That literal alternate label is preserved rather than silently replaced with another phonetic character.
The source phrase “formant pulse” describes the simplified filtering illustration. The teaching explains frequency-dependent emphasis without treating a formant as a separate sound-generating pulse.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches
teaching: The columns hold four vowel filters fixed, with schwa /ə/, /u/, /i/ or /I/, and /a/ shown in order. Their target frequencies are 500 and 1500 Hz, then 300, 1000 and 2000 Hz, then 300 and 2200 Hz, and finally 800 and 900 Hz. Moving down a column changes source F0 rather than changing that column’s vocal-tract shape.

The source rows are labelled heavy or loose with F0 100, lighter or tighter with F0 250, and lightest or tightest with F0 350. Across each row, the same harmonic spacing samples different filters. Within each column, the smooth pale envelope and dashed red formant targets stay in place while the colored harmonic stems become farther apart.

At F0 100, many harmonics lie under each broad resonance region and trace its shape densely. The schwa and /i/ comparisons retain a low-frequency group and a separate higher-frequency group. The /u/ comparison has three favored regions, and the nearby /a/ targets form a closely grouped region. The high number of available stems makes these shapes easier to recognize.

At F0 250, there are fewer samples of each envelope. A resonance can lie between neighboring harmonics, so the strongest visible stem may sit beside its target. At F0 350, the gaps are wider still. A favored region can have few nearby harmonics, and two close resonances can be difficult to distinguish from the sparse stems.

The frequency windows extend to 4k Hz. Horizontal stem position identifies an actual harmonic frequency, while height represents its strength after filtering. The dashed red ticks identify the filter targets rather than additional generated harmonics. A formant becoming hard to read in a sparse spectrum does not mean the vocal-tract resonance itself moved or disappeared.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram
teaching: A spectrum represents the frequency components of a short instant. Its horizontal direction is frequency and its stem height represents amplitude. The six small spectra give three successive /i/ examples followed by three /a/ examples, allowing the frequency pattern and relative heights to be compared over time.

A spectrogram places many spectra beside one another as time advances. Frequency becomes the vertical direction, labelled in Hz from 0 through 1000, 2000 and 3000 to about 4000. Time runs horizontally toward the right. A frequency that would lie farther right in a spectrum appears higher in the spectrogram.

Amplitude changes its visual role as well. A tall spectral component becomes a dark mark at its frequency and time. High amplitude is black, medium amplitude is gray, and low amplitude is white. Height in a spectrum therefore maps to darkness in a spectrogram, rather than to the vertical location of a spectrogram band.

The /ia/ illustration moves from /i/ on the left to /a/ on the right. The lowest strong band rises from a few hundred Hz to below 1000 Hz. The next strong band falls from a region above 2000 Hz toward a region a little above 1000 Hz. A higher band near 3000 Hz also shifts downward, while an upper faint band stays in the higher-frequency region. The bands curve during the transition because the favored frequency regions change over time.

The small /i/ spectra emphasize a low group and a separated higher-frequency group, while the /a/ spectra arrange their stronger components differently. Turning those successive amplitude patterns into dark vertical frequency slices creates continuous-looking bands. sections.title: Use formants as input to vowel recognition
teaching: Formants provide a numerical description of the frequency regions favored by a vocal-tract shape. The proposed recognition task uses students’ formant measurements as input and asks a neural network to decide which vowel was spoken. This connects the physical resonances of speech to a learning problem, mapping a numerical sound description to a category.
The stated aim is to train the network on those measurements. It is a plan for learning a recognition mapping, rather than a report of measured classification accuracy or a completed trained model.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network
teaching: The network receives two inputs, F1 and F2. They supply a pair of formant measurements rather than an entire speech waveform. The information passes through three hidden layers containing 3, 2 and 4 neurons, and then reaches 5 output neurons.

Every neuron in a layer connects to every neuron in the following layer. Each receiving unit combines incoming values according to its connection weights. The result becomes an input to the next layer, so the flow proceeds from two measurements through successive internal representations toward five candidate word labels.

The output labels, in top-to-bottom order, are /done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/ and /Dan/. Each label is associated with a distinct output unit. Keeping that order is necessary when interpreting a five-value output.

The network is explicitly purely linear, with no activation functions between its layers. A unit’s weighted result is passed onward without an additional nonlinear transformation. Adding several such layers changes the sequence of weighted combinations, but it does not by itself provide a rule that turns the final numbers into probabilities.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections
teaching: The displayed input pair is F1 = 320 and F2 = 2000. Before training, each connection receives a random weight between −1 and 1. A weight controls how an incoming value contributes to the receiving neuron. Positive and negative weights allow contributions to reinforce or oppose one another, while magnitude controls the size of that contribution.

Read the neurons in each layer from top to bottom. The connections from F1 to the three first-hidden-layer neurons carry [−0.35, −0.70, 0.30]. Those from F2 carry [−0.86, 0.07, −0.27]. These six separate weights let the same pair of input measurements be combined differently by the three receiving neurons.

From the first hidden layer to the two neurons in the second hidden layer, the top source neuron has weights [−0.88, 0.01], the middle source neuron has [−0.93, −0.13], and the bottom source neuron has [−0.86, −0.82]. Each pair is ordered by the top and bottom receiving neuron. These are six further connections.

From the second hidden layer to the four neurons in the third hidden layer, the top source neuron has weights [−0.15, 0.65, −0.75, −0.55], and the bottom source neuron has [0.25, 0.90, 0.15, −0.21]. Each list follows the four receiving neurons from top to bottom, preserving all eight connections.

For the final connections, use the output order /done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/, /Dan/. The top neuron in the third hidden layer has outgoing weights [0.95, −0.91, 0.72, −0.42, −0.71]. The second has [−0.76, −0.38, 0.63, −0.64, 0.16]. The third has [0.28, −0.26, 0.10, −0.87, −0.88]. The bottom has [−0.59, 0.36, −0.14, −0.37, 0.17]. These twenty weights provide different combinations for the five candidates.

The architecture therefore has forty weighted connections, grouped as six, six, eight and twenty across the four layer transitions. Their displayed values are an initialization, not evidence of learned knowledge. The internal neurons have no printed numerical activations, so the picture identifies the connections and inputs without supplying a worked numerical forward pass.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution
teaching: Forward flow uses the current weights to carry information from the two formant inputs through the first, second and third hidden layers to the output layer. Each layer receives the values produced by the preceding layer and combines them through its own connections. This describes inference with the available weights, rather than a training update that changes them.

The displayed p(word) bars use the order /done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/, /Dan/ and values [0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.2]. In that illustration, /done/ has the largest assigned value, /Dan/ is next, and the other three candidates have equal smaller values. The five displayed numbers form a normalized distribution.

The purely linear declaration does not supply the operation that makes arbitrary weighted outputs nonnegative and normalized. The bars therefore illustrate the intended kind of categorical output rather than a verified numerical result of the random weights and the input pair. A drawn probability distribution and a demonstrated computation of that distribution are different pieces of evidence.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch
teaching: The code imports torch and imports torch.nn under the shorter name nn. The second import supplies the neural-network layer classes and the Sequential container used to assemble the model. The variable net is assigned that assembled sequence.

The comment identifies the purely linear architecture as 2 → 3 → 2 → 4 → 5. Inside nn.Sequential, nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False) maps the two inputs to the first three hidden units. nn.Linear(3, 2, bias=False) maps those three values to two. nn.Linear(2, 4, bias=False) expands the next representation to four values. nn.Linear(4, 5, bias=False) produces five output values, one for each labelled candidate.

For nn.Linear, the first argument is the number of incoming values and the second is the number of outgoing values. Each layer stores one row of weights per receiving unit and one column per incoming value. The four weight-matrix sizes are therefore 3 by 2, 2 by 3, 4 by 2 and 5 by 4. Matching the output size of one layer with the input size of the next allows their values to flow through the sequence.

The bias=False argument removes a separately added bias from every layer. There are no activation-function layers between the Linear calls, so each layer passes its linear result directly to the next. The sequence expresses the connections and layer sizes in executable model declarations without adding an unshown probability-normalization step.

The supplied code declares the model only. It does not provide a formant tensor to net, assign the forty displayed example weights, compare an output with a target, calculate a loss or perform a training update. It therefore establishes the architecture, while leaving the proposed learning task and any resulting classification performance unexecuted.
